newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Prince Sultan denies going to U.S. for arms.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Prince Sultan denies going to U.S. for arms.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's defence minister on Tuesday denied reports he was travelling to the United States to clinch a military aircraft deal, saying his visit was designed to discuss regional issues with the new administration.
Defence and Aviation Minister Prince Sultan is due to visit Paris on February 22 and continue on to Washington for talks with newly-appointed U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen and other officials.

"I am sure you heard the international press saying that Sultan will visit the United States looking for an aircraft deal," Prince Sultan said in a speech at the King Faisal airbase in the northern city of Tabuk. The speech was carried by the official Saudi news agency SPA.
"Whatever has been said about discussions or arms deals during this visit bears no truth whatsoever," he said.

The United States said last month that Saudi Arabia was shopping for jet fighters, but reacted cautiously to a report that Riyadh would buy up to 100 Lockheed Martin Corp F-16s in a multibillion-dollar deal.
U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said the Saudis were seeking replacements for their ageing fleet of 114 F-5 fighters bought from the United States.
Prince Sultan admitted the kingdom was looking for a substitute for its F-5s.
"For two years we have been looking for a replacement for the F-5s," he said. "Experts at the airforce decided that F-16s are a good replacement for the F-5s."

But he said the issue would not be discussed during the trip to the United States, which would only focus on discussing the new Clinton administration's strategies in the region, the Arab World and particularly Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally.

"Distorting the visit by asking to sign an aircraft deal would not be right. We will not discuss this at all and this will never happen. If we want to do something, we will do it in our own country," he said.
The United States is Saudi Arabia's biggest arms supplier, followed by Britain and France. Saudi Arabia already has a variety of U.S. arms on order worth $25 billion until the end of the century.
Diplomats say a fighter package would help ease tension between Riyadh and Washington after two bombings in Saudi Arabia in little over a year that have killed 24 Americans.
